c.tagline: The 'Emerald Isle of the Caribbean' — Irish heritage, a buried city, and a live volcano.

taxi.fareNote: No ride-hailing apps; taxis charge government-set fixed fares (published by the tourist board). Self-drive rental cars require a temporary local driving permit, and Montserrat drives on the left.

emergency.note: 911 and 999 both reach police, fire, and ambulance. The East Caribbean dollar is fixed at EC$2.70 to US$1, and US dollars are widely accepted.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: The volcanic Exclusion Zone covering the island's south (including buried Plymouth) is off-limits without authorization due to Soufrière Hills volcano hazards.

hood_desc: The bustling de facto capital in the island's safe northwest, home to government offices, the bank, shops, the post office, and the Montserrat Tourist Board; the practical hub for business and services.

The emerging new capital and main seaport where the ferry from Antigua docks, with a festival village, cultural centre, and the island's beach-lined northwest tip; the arrival point and future town centre.
A lively village to the south near the edge of the volcanic exclusion zone, with restaurants, bars, dive operators, and the road up to the Montserrat Volcano Observatory; a favourite visitor base.
A quiet residential and villa area on the west coast known for Woodlands Beach and sea-turtle nesting; suits travelers wanting calm and black-sand shores.
A leafy upscale enclave of villas and expat homes near Olveston House restaurant; relaxed and green, ideal for longer villa stays.

water.note: Spring-fed tap water is clean and safe to drink.

transit.hours: Privately run minibuses operate mainly during daylight, most frequently morning and afternoon, with little service on Sundays.
transit.note: Montserrat has no formal timetabled transit. Green-plate 'H'-registered minibuses ply the main road between the northern villages for a small fixed fare, but most visitors rely on taxis or a rental car, as the island is hilly and spread out.
transit.pay: Pay the minibus driver in cash (EC or US dollars) on boarding; fares are just a couple of EC dollars.

ferry: Jaden Sun ferry to/from Antigua (Little Bay)

transit.m: Taxi to Brades and the northern villages (~10 min, government-set fares)
Many guesthouses and villas arrange complimentary airport transfers

tip.r: A service charge of ~10% is often added at hotels and restaurants; otherwise ~10% is appreciated for good service.

food.name: Goat water
food.desc: Montserrat's national dish: goat stewed for hours with cloves, thyme, rum and a dark roux until thick, eaten with a crusty roll to mop the bowl.

places.name: Emerald Rose Restaurant
places.note: Local and West Indian cooking; goat water and souse are the weekend specials here.

places.name: The Attic
places.note: Casual local spot in the de-facto capital, well liked in recent write-ups for hearty island plates.

places.name: Hilltop Coffee House and Family Centre
places.note: Community kitchen doing home-style island food; ask what pot is on that day.

food.name: Saltfish and roast breadfruit
food.desc: Salted cod flaked and sauteed with onion, sweet pepper and thyme, served with breadfruit roasted over coals or with fried bakes. The classic island breakfast.

places.name: Emerald Rose Restaurant
places.note: Dependable for traditional plates; saltfish appears on the local-food side of the menu.

places.name: Hilltop Coffee House and Family Centre
places.note: Good for an early, unfussy local breakfast before heading out for the day.

food.name: Souse
food.desc: Pork or chicken feet cured in a sharp cold broth of lime, cucumber, onion and hot pepper. A weekend dish, usually eaten standing up with friends.

places.name: Emerald Rose Restaurant
places.note: Souse alongside goat water on the weekend specials board; go on a Friday or Saturday.

places.name: Brades roadside weekend stands
places.note: Pop-up tables near the shops sell souse and barbecue on Friday nights; cash only.

food.name: Fresh grilled fish and seafood
food.desc: Snapper, mahi mahi and lobster landed at Little Bay and Carr's Bay, grilled whole with lime, garlic and pepper sauce and served with rice and peas.

places.name: Soca Cabana
places.note: Beach bar and restaurant right on the sand at Little Bay; grilled fish and sunset drinks.

places.name: Little Bay fish landing
places.note: Boats come in through the afternoon; nearby cooks grill what the fishers have brought up.

places.name: Olveston House
places.note: Long-standing guesthouse dining room with a set menu that leans on the day's catch.

food.name: Sunday barbecue ribs and chicken
food.desc: Open-grill lunches of jerked ribs, chicken and fish with macaroni pie and provisions. Sunday cook-ups are the island's main social meal of the week.

places.name: Soca Cabana
places.note: Sunday open-grill lunch on the beach is a fixture of the local week; go early.

places.name: The Attic
places.note: Weekend grill plates and a friendly local crowd; portions are generous.

food.name: Mountain chicken (heritage dish)
food.desc: The giant ditch frog was once Montserrat's prized delicacy, but disease and habitat loss made it critically endangered and it is now protected, not eaten.

places.name: Montserrat National Trust
places.note: Exhibits explain the frog's story and the recovery programme; the place to learn rather than taste.

places.name: Emerald Rose Restaurant
places.note: Older cooks here remember how it was prepared; goat water is the dish that took its place.

food.name: Homemade ginger beer
food.desc: Fresh ginger grated, steeped and lightly fermented with lime and brown sugar until it bites. Sold cold in reused bottles and brewed strong at Christmas.

places.name: Brades shops and roadside stands
places.note: Home-brewed bottles sold near the shops; ask for it cold, and expect real heat.

places.name: Hilltop Coffee House and Family Centre
places.note: Local juices and ginger beer made in-house alongside the coffee and food.

food.name: Montserrat rum punch
food.desc: Dark rum shaken with lime, cane syrup, nutmeg and island fruit juice. Bottled local punches are a common souvenir as well as a bar staple.

places.name: Soca Cabana
places.note: Beachfront bar mixing punches at sunset; the most relaxed drink on the island.

places.name: Olveston House bar
places.note: Quiet colonial-era veranda bar; a calmer setting for a punch before dinner.

landmarks: Soufrière Hills Volcano
The still-steaming volcano that reshaped Montserrat in the 1990s dominates the island's south, its lava dome visible from viewpoints across the safe zone.
Plymouth (Buried City)
Montserrat's abandoned capital, entombed in ash like a modern Pompeii, can be glimpsed on guided exclusion-zone tours past church spires rising from grey mudflows.
Montserrat Volcano Observatory
The working observatory above Salem pairs a fascinating visitor center and documentary film with the island's best safe view of the Soufrière Hills dome.
Jack Boy Hill Viewpoint
This landscaped eastern lookout surveys the ash-buried former airport and pyroclastic flows spilling to the sea, with telescopes and a picnic-friendly garden.
Garibaldi Hill
A rugged hilltop drive or hike ending in haunting panoramas over ruined Plymouth, Richmond Hill and the volcano beyond, Montserrat's most sobering photo stop.
Little Bay Beach
The island's emerging new capital area curves around a dark-sand harbor beach with beach bars, dive shops and ferries arriving beneath green cliffs.
Montserrat National Trust Botanic Garden
In Olveston near Brades, the National Trust's garden showcases native orchids, medicinal plants and the endemic Montserrat oriole story alongside heritage exhibits.
Oriole Walkway Trail (Centre Hills)
This rainforest trail through the protected Centre Hills climbs to Lawyers Mountain, prime territory for spotting the endemic Montserrat oriole, the national bird.
Runaway Ghaut
Legend promises that whoever drinks from this roadside spring will return to Montserrat, making the shaded ravine an obligatory sip for departing visitors.
Carr's Bay Gun Battery
A 17th-century coastal fortification near Brades with weathered cannons still aimed out to sea, overlooking a golden-sand bay on Montserrat's north coast.

train.note: Montserrat has never had a railway. The island's airport was destroyed by the Soufrière Hills eruption; the replacement John A. Osborne Airport in the north takes small aircraft from Antigua. Otherwise you arrive by ferry.

bus.note: No international coaches. Montserrat has a small minibus service running along the northern road between Brades, Salem and Little Bay, plus taxis - the southern two-thirds of the island remains an exclusion zone around the volcano and is closed to unescorted travel. Guided tours are the way to see it.

intl.to: Antigua - Saint John's - from Little Bay, ~90 min
intl.op: Montserrat ferry service — check current schedules with the Montserrat Port Authority

ferry.note: The Antigua ferry from Little Bay is Montserrat's main link to the outside world alongside the small plane, running several days a week when in service - the operator and schedule have changed repeatedly over the years, so confirm before travelling. It is an international crossing, so carry your passport. Crossings are cancelled in rough seas.

half.name: Jack Boy Hill & Exclusion Zone viewpoint
half.blurb: Overlook the buried former capital of Plymouth and the smoking Soufrière Hills volcano.

half.name: Rendezvous Bay
half.blurb: The island's only white-sand beach, reached by a coastal hike over the hill or by boat.

full.name: Antigua
full.blurb: Beaches and historic St. John's, about 90 minutes away by ferry from Little Bay.
